titulo.texto: Traditional Three-Piece Mestiza Dress of Yucatán

frase_gancho.texto: Three white pieces embroidered with flowers, made for dancing the jarana in Yucatán.

puente_narrativo.texto: From what people wear, we move on to where they live. Look for a house of palm and wood, with rounded corners, hammocks hanging inside, and a garden all around.

guion_corto.texto: This three-piece set is called a terno, and it is the formal dress of the women of Yucatán. It is made up of the huipil, a white dress that hangs straight; the jubón, a square piece that covers the shoulders and chest; and the fustán, a petticoat that reaches the ankles. The edges of all three pieces carry hand embroidery in cross-stitch, with roses, tulips and orchids in red, yellow, turquoise and violet, and they are finished with white lace. It is worn at the vaquerías, which are the dance festivals of the towns, and also at weddings and at patron saint festivals. It is a dress that brings together the elegance, the joy and the coolness that the heat of the peninsula calls for.

guion_largo.texto:
The vaquerías were born on the haciendas, when cattle were gathered to be branded, and over time they became the great festival of the peninsula. Today they begin with a Mass and continue with an orchestra of brass and percussion that plays the jarana, the dance music of Yucatán. Couples stamp their feet with short, light steps, and the women, in their ternos, seem to glide across the floor.

There is a custom that is never forgotten. In the middle of the dance, someone shouts “¡bomba!” and the music stops. Then a dancer recites an improvised verse, almost always with humor, and everyone applauds. After that, the orchestra starts up again as if nothing had happened. It is a way of conversing in verse, between the music and the dance.

Here is a curiosity: in Yucatán the word “mestiza” has a meaning of its own. It is usually used to name the woman, almost always from a Maya family, who wears the huipil, so it speaks more about the dress and the way of life than about a mixture. That is why you will find the name “terno de mestiza” in every museum and in every town of the peninsula.

The word huipil comes from Nahuatl, but the garment is much older than the Mexica. The long tunics of the Maya figures of Jaina, and those of the characters painted on vessels and in murals, look very much like it. In other words, the white dress you see here has more than a thousand years of history behind it, with changes in fashion and adornment, but with a form that can still be recognized.

The embroidery is called xokbil chuy, which means “counted thread.” It is cross-stitch: the embroiderer counts the threads of the cloth and places one cross after another, until they form roses and little birds that look painted. A well-embroidered terno can take months of work, and the patterns are passed from mothers to daughters. There is also machine embroidery, but the handmade kind is still the most valued. Because each embroiderer chooses her own flowers and colors, no two ternos are exactly alike, and at a single dance you will see different gardens moving in time to the music.

The terno blends two worlds. The straight tunic and the handwork come from the Maya tradition, while the bobbin lace and some adornments arrived with the Spanish. To all this are added the jewels: a rosary of gold filigree, often inherited from the family, that falls over the chest. If you look closely, there are centuries of exchange in a single dress.

Just like the [Papantla costume](mna_s18_traje_papantla), the white of Yucatán answers to the heat: it reflects the sun and cools the body. But here the white is the canvas of a garden. The embroidered flowers, which never wither, are a way of wearing spring all year round.

Behind every terno there is a woman who embroidered it, another who inherited it, and many who wear it at the festival. It is a garment that stays alive because it is danced in: it is not kept in a display case, it comes out to the plaza every time the jarana plays.

texto.Technique/Material: Linen/cotton embroidered in cross-stitch (xokbilchuy), bobbin lace and filigree
texto.Function: Formal attire for the Cattle Festival, weddings and patron saint celebrations

texto.pregunta: Myth: Traditional costumes are just museum disguises.
texto.respuesta: Reality: The terno is still worn today at the vaquerías, weddings and patron saint festivals of Yucatán.
